claim: A capture now records which document it was served, derived from marks it already carried. Replayed over fourteen captures taken 2026-09-09, the fingerprint separated calendly's four captures of a Google sign-in wall from its two of the real page by 97.6% on its worst field — without reading `targetMatch`, the field that names the fault, at all.
boardClaim: The tool can now tell when two runs describe different pages, and it found the case it was built for without being told where to look.
evidence: For two days this project compared measurements of one page against a census of a different one and could not see it: a capture's own probes navigate — a consent wall, a sign-in redirect — and the count of what is on the page was taken afterwards. Four calendly captures reported one heading and five links; the page has forty-two headings and one hundred and fifty-three. Nothing said so, because nothing recorded WHICH document a capture had described. #687 gave every capture that identity, DERIVED from marks already on disk rather than stored as a new field — so the fourteen captures taken before it existed acquired one too, and the claim below could be tested against real recordings rather than against new ones. Replayed 2026-09-09: the fingerprint puts the four wall captures and the two real ones 97.6% apart on their worst field, and — the part that matters — it does so from element counts alone, never reading `domCensus.targetMatch`, the field that names the fault. An independent instrument agreeing with a known answer is worth more than one told what to look for. The same replay bounds what the measure is good for: two pages that did NOT change between captures still differ by 1.6% and 2.5% on their worst field, which is ordinary page jitter — a carousel, a lazy image — so an exact match is not the test and a tolerance has to be chosen from a measured distribution before this is used as a gate. Between 2.5% and 97.6% today's data shows nothing at all. (`documentIdentity` from #687/#722, replayed by `orchestrator` over `runs/witness/` on 2026-09-09; the two files the 97.6% is computed from are `runs/witness/2026-09-09T08-12-27-003Z-calendly-com.json` and `runs/witness/2026-09-09T12-49-29-716Z-calendly-com.json`, field `domCensus`; four points on two pages is where the jitter figure comes from and it is not a distribution.)
affirmed: Measured by me, on captures I took, on the fleet I drive. The 97.6% is `documentIdentity`'s worst field across the two named files; the 1.6% and 2.5% are hubspot (3 captures) and ikea (2 captures) on the same afternoon. WHAT I AM NOT CLAIMING: that jitter is always ~2%. Two pages on one afternoon is four points, not a distribution, and `theregister.com` at 1,471 links is exactly the shape that might break the figure. The fleet run that would settle it is #688, whose acceptance I have changed to require the tolerance be chosen from measured jitter BEFORE the run — because run as an exact match it would have reported near-100% variation on every page and meant nothing.
